Rebuilding the design
foundation of ResumeHelp

The product had grown but the design hadn't. I led the migration from an inconsistent, accessibility-challenged theme to a proper design system used by the whole team.

Context

Why this project happened

ResumeHelp is an online resume builder. As the product grew — more pages, more markets, more people working on it — the original design started showing cracks. It was never built as a system. Just a collection of one-off decisions made over time.

01

Felt outdated

The visual style no longer matched where the brand was heading.

02

Hard to scale

No shared rules — every designer made their own calls.

03

Dev confusion

No specs meant developers couldn't build a proper component library.

04

Accessibility gaps

Some colours didn't meet basic contrast standards.

Design Systems Accessibility Consistency Agency Collaboration Developer Handoff
The Problem

6 things that were quietly broken

None of these were show-stoppers alone. Together, they made the product feel patched together — and made designing new pages without adding more inconsistency nearly impossible.

01

Poor colour contrast

White text on the primary green (#3CD9A7) failed WCAG standards. A real issue for a mass-use product.

02

Colour overlays everywhere

Every hero section had a dark teal overlay on photos. Images lost their purpose.

03

No spacing or grid system

No defined margins, no grid, no padding rules. Every page was eyeballed.

04

Thin typography

Only 6 type styles for the whole product — not enough for pages of this complexity.

05

Inconsistent icons

Outlined on one page, filled on another, 2-colour somewhere else. No rule at all.

06

Dark sections without logic

Dark backgrounds used randomly to "separate" sections — no system, just habit.

Before

The old theme

Teal-heavy, dark overlays on everything, no defined spacing. It worked — but not at scale.

After

The new design system

A proper system — colour tokens, grid specs, button rules, blade backgrounds, and a full typography hierarchy. Built to scale.

Structured colour palette with named tokens
Blade backgrounds — 3 light, 3 dark, each used with purpose
12-col desktop · 8-col tablet · 2-col mobile
Full button system — 5 types × 4 sizes × all states
Key Change · Colours

Fixing the colour problem first

The old green wasn't just outdated — it was failing accessibility. That made it the most urgent thing to fix. The new system moved to a violet-led palette where every colour pairing was checked for contrast compliance.

Key Change · Typography

A font change that changed the feel

Typography is one of the first things a user notices — even if they don't realise it. The old fonts felt wide and heavy. The new ones feel modern, clean, and approachable. A small change on paper, but a big shift in how the product feels.

Before — Old Fonts
Montserrat (headings) · Source Sans Pro (body) — functional but wide and heavy
After — New Fonts
Circular STD (headings) · Public Sans (body) — rounder, friendlier, more modern
Old · Headings
Montserrat
Wide letterforms, felt bulky at large sizes
New · Headings
Circular STD
Rounder, warmer — feels premium and approachable
Old · Body
Source Sans Pro
Decent readability but generic for a product of this scale
New · Body
Public Sans
Clean, neutral, highly readable — works well at all sizes

💡 Why it matters: ResumeHelp's users are job seekers — often stressed, often in a hurry. A friendlier, more readable typeface makes the product feel less intimidating. That's a UX decision, not just a visual one.

Design Decisions

What I reviewed, shaped & enforced

The agency built the initial system. My job was to review critically, push back where needed, iterate, and apply it across the product.

🎨

Colour — accessibility first

Replaced the failing green with a violet-led palette. Every colour pairing checked for WCAG contrast before finalising.

🔤

Typography — personality shift

Moved from Montserrat + Source Sans Pro to Circular STD + Public Sans. Rounder, friendlier, and more readable — especially at body size across long pages.

📐

Grid — finally defined

12-col desktop (1280px max), 8-col tablet, 2-col mobile. For the first time, layouts had real rules.

🧩

Blade backgrounds — with purpose

6 background options defined. Dark sections now had a reason — not just "to separate things." Pages felt considered, not assembled.

🔘

Buttons — fully specced for dev handoff

5 types, 4 sizes, 3 breakpoints. Padding, min-width, hover/disabled states — all documented. No more guessing.

✅

Consistency reviews — catching drift early

When agency pages came in slightly off — wrong padding, heading size different — I caught and fixed it before it reached developers.

My Role

How I worked with the agency

The agency created the initial system. I owned the outcome — reviewing everything, shaping decisions through multiple rounds, making final calls, and applying the system to the actual product.

Step 01

Agency proposes

Agency creates first version of the design system.

Step 02

I review

Check against product needs — consistency, accessibility, feasibility.

Step 03

Iterate

Push back, ask for changes, do some edits myself. Repeat until right.

Step 04

Apply & govern

Use system across 10–25 pages. Make sure everyone follows it.

💡 In most companies, this is how it works. Design systems are rarely built alone. Knowing how to evaluate, shape, and govern one — that's the real skill.

Outcome

What actually changed

No A/B test numbers — and I'll be honest about that. But the changes were real and visible across the team and the product.

✓

Accessibility fixed. The contrast issue with the old green was resolved. Every colour pairing in the new system passes WCAG AA.

✓

Designers could move faster. With a shared system, no one had to reinvent spacing or colours on each new page.

✓

Developers got real specs. Exact grid values, button padding, colour tokens — everything they needed to build a component library.

✓

Applied to 10–25 pages. The system wasn't just documented — I used it. Every page I worked on after this was built on the same foundation.

✓

One source of truth. Designers, developers, and the agency — all working from the same system. Reviews became faster because there was now a clear standard to check against.

Reflection

What I learnt

This was my first time working at a systems level — thinking about how design decisions affect the whole product, not just one page.

💡

Document the "why", not just the "what"

Rules without reasoning don't survive. When I couldn't explain why a decision was made, it got questioned. Writing it down early saves a lot of time.

♿

Accessibility should come first, not last

We caught the contrast issue during review. Ideally it should be part of the brief from the start — before colours are even picked.

🛡️

Owning a system means protecting it

Building the system was the easier part. Making sure everyone followed it consistently — that was the real work.

"Design systems aren't about control. They're about giving everyone the freedom to move fast without breaking things."

— Personal reflection on this project
